title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: TikTok trend
drivers.evidence: No past occurrence of TikTok trend. Noise-adjusted effect of similar virality is x1.15, but evidence is thin. Not enough to justify full uplift.

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: 2026-09-28: price $6.56 → sales 24 units (x0.45 vs baseline). Price rise at same level led to 55% drop. This week likely similar.

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 44.9. No events or promotions in target week. Price increased 2.3% (to $6.56), which historically correlates with a dip (2026-09-28: 24 units, x0.45 vs baseline). TikTok trend is a new driver with no past equivalent; noise-adjusted effect is uncertain. Recent weeks show no sustained lift at this price. Classical uplift model gives 1.00, but this ignores the TikTok signal. We shrink the potential lift toward 1.0 due to lack of precedent. Downside risk from price increase and no promotion justifies widening downside spread slightly.

brief:
PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-18 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)
  planner notes: Product is trending on TikTok

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.9 | 5%-95%: 20.2 - 68.2 | 10%-90%: 26.8 - 64.8

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
